title: Acts 18:1–17
context: In Corinth Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers expelled from Rome, and reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath. When opposition grows, he turns to the Gentiles and teaches next door in the house of Titius Justus; the synagogue ruler Crispus and many Corinthians believe. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid, for no one will harm him and he has many people in this city, so Paul stays eighteen months. When opponents bring him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about Jewish law.

verses.text: After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth. Arminian readers see him moving to a busy, morally troubled city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God sending him where many of his people are.

verses.text: He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them,
verses.arminianNotes: He meets Aquila and Priscilla, Jews expelled from Rome under Claudius. Arminian commentators see God connecting believers through ordinary events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see providence using an imperial edict.

verses.text: and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.
verses.arminianNotes: He works with them as a tentmaker. Arminian readers see Paul supporting himself so the gospel is free.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see dignity in ordinary work.

verses.text: He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath and persuaded Jews and Greeks.
verses.arminianNotes: He reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath, persuading Jews and Greeks. Arminian expositors see persuasion aimed at decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see faithful use of means.

verses.text: When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.
verses.arminianNotes: When Silas and Timothy arrive, Paul devotes himself fully to the word. Arminian readers see support freeing him for ministry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word as Paul’s central calling.

verses.text: When they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!”
verses.arminianNotes: When they oppose him, he shakes out his clothes: “Your blood be on your own heads.” Arminian commentators see their responsibility for refusing the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see Paul released from responsibility after faithful witness, as in Ezekiel 33.

verses.text: He departed there and went into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
verses.arminianNotes: He goes next door to the house of Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. Arminian readers see the mission continuing nearby.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing a new base.

verses.text: Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized.
verses.arminianNotes: Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes with his household, and many Corinthians believe and are baptized. Arminian expositors see hearing, believing, and baptism in sequence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see whole households brought into the church.

verses.text: The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent;
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord says, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent.” Arminian readers see encouragement given to a weary servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ sustaining his messenger.

verses.text: for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I am with you, and no one will harm you, for I have many people in this city.” Arminian readers see “many people” as those God foreknew would believe in response to Paul’s preaching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a strong text for election: Christ already calls them “my people” before they have believed, which is why Paul should keep preaching.

verses.text: He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
verses.arminianNotes: He stays eighteen months teaching the word. Arminian commentators see sustained ministry building a church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s promise motivating patient labor.

verses.text: But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
verses.arminianNotes: Under Gallio, opponents bring Paul to the judgment seat. Arminian readers see the promise of protection tested.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God keeping his word through a Roman official.

verses.text: saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”
verses.arminianNotes: They accuse him of persuading people to worship contrary to the law. Arminian expositors see a charge meant to make Christianity illegal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the gospel’s relation to Judaism at stake.

verses.text: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you;
verses.arminianNotes: Before Paul can speak, Gallio says he would hear a case of actual wrongdoing. Arminian readers see a ruler refusing to be used.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s protection without Paul even needing to speak.

verses.text: but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.”
verses.arminianNotes: Questions of words and names and their own law are not his concern. Arminian commentators see Rome treating the faith as a Jewish matter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see providence granting legal space to the church.

verses.text: So he drove them from the judgment seat.
verses.arminianNotes: He drives them from the judgment seat. Arminian readers see the accusers dismissed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Lord’s promise of verse 10 fulfilled.

verses.text: Then all the Greeks seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd beats Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, while Gallio ignores it. Arminian expositors see disorder unchecked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors note that a Sosthenes later appears as a believer in 1 Corinthians 1:1, perhaps the same man.
